title: Issue types in agile
blurb: Classify an issue as a request for change, off-specification, problem or business opportunity, and explain why agile embraces change.
question: During an iteration, a product is found that will not meet its agreed quality specification. What type of issue is this, and how does an agile project view change in general?

teach.h: What the issues practice is for
teach.body: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project's baseline. An issue is an event relevant to the project that needs project management consideration, and anyone can raise one at any time. It has already happened, unlike a risk, which is uncertain. The question the practice answers is simple: what now, when something deviates from what was agreed, and how do we respond?
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 11.1; PRINCE2 7 manual 10.1

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: A proposal to change a baseline
Users ask for a new feature
A product that will not meet its quality spec
A screen fails its agreed standard
teach.caption: Book reference: 11.3.1.

teach.h: Which type of issue is it?

children.edge: A product will miss its spec
children.label: Off-specification

teach.body: Working iteratively and incrementally produces many versions of the product, so change is inevitable. PRINCE2 Agile tailors the issue management approach to say that this change should be embraced and supported, not resisted. New learning from users after each increment is a sign the process is working. What matters is handling each change at the right level, so the team is not slowed by needless formality.

teach.h: Handled at the lowest sensible level

teach.body: Issues that do not affect the agreed baseline can be handled informally at team level, usually by the team and product owner. Issues that do affect the baseline must be handled and decided formally at the appropriate management level: the project board, or whoever has delegated authority for changes. The next lessons look at baseline versus detail change and at the team techniques for absorbing change.

Project manager Imogen Clarke runs an agile project for a new depot tracking app. In one week four issues arrive. Drivers ask to add photo proof of delivery: a request for change. A barcode screen fails its agreed accessibility standard: an off-specification. The mapping supplier announces it is closing: a problem. The finance team offers extra money for a tablet version: a business opportunity. Imogen and product owner Musa Diallo first ask of each one: does it change the project backlog?

teach.text: A business opportunity is still an issue: an issue is not only bad news. And an issue has already happened, while a risk is an uncertain event that may happen. Also, 'change' is a V1 and PRINCE2 6th-edition theme name; in V2 this is the issues practice.

items: Issues practice: collect and assess issues and control changes to the baseline.
Types defined in 11.3.1: request for change, off-specification, problem, business opportunity.
Request for change: a proposal to change a baseline.
Off-specification: a product that will not meet its quality specification.
Agile: multiple versions mean inevitable change, embraced and supported (Table 11.1).
No baseline effect: informal, team level. Baseline effect: formal, management level.

summary: You can now classify issues as a request for change, off-specification, problem or business opportunity, and explain that agile treats change as expected and to be embraced. You can also say that issues are handled informally at team level unless they affect the baseline.

options: A proposal to change an agreed baseline
A product that will not meet its quality specification
An issue with an immediate and negative impact
An unexpected positive consequence for the project
A.why: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: A proposal to change a baseline is a request for change.
whyNot.2: An issue with immediate negative impact is a problem.
whyNot.3: An unexpected positive consequence is a business opportunity.

A.q: Partway through a project, the sponsor's organization unexpectedly offers additional funding. What type of issue is this?
A.why: An unanticipated positive consequence for the project or user organization, such as extra funding, is a business opportunity (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline; funding becoming available is not a proposal.
whyNot.1: A problem has an immediate negative impact; this is positive.
whyNot.2: An off-specification concerns a product missing its quality specification.

A.q: What is the purpose of the issues practice?
options: To collect and assess issues and control changes to the baseline
To identify, assess and control uncertainties that may occur
To compare actual achievements with those that were planned
To define who is accountable and responsible for decisions
A.why: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project's baseline (11.1).

whyNot.1: Managing uncertainties is the purpose of the risk practice.
whyNot.2: Comparing achievements against plans is the progress practice.
whyNot.3: Defining accountability and responsibilities is the organization practice.

B.q: The company supplying a key component goes bankrupt during the second stage. What type of issue is this?
B.why: A problem is an issue with an immediate and negative impact, such as a supplier going bankrupt (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: A business opportunity is a positive consequence, not a supplier failure.
whyNot.2: No one is proposing a change to a baseline; the event itself is harmful.
whyNot.3: No product has been found to miss its quality specification.

B.q:
Which two statements about issues in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Change is seen as inevitable and should be embraced and supported.
2. Every issue is referred to the project board for a decision.
3. Issues that do not affect the baseline can be handled informally at team level.
4. A business opportunity is an issue with a negative consequence.
B.why: Agile embraces inevitable change (1), and issues without baseline impact are handled informally at team level (3) (Table 11.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: issues within the baseline are handled at team level.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: most issues stay at team level, and a business opportunity is positive.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: a business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence.

B.q: Users ask for an extra feature to be added to the product during delivery. What type of issue is this?
B.why: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline; requests for change usually come from users as new or changed requirements (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: Nothing has failed its quality specification; users want something new.
whyNot.1: A business opportunity is an unexpected benefit arising, not a request for a feature.
whyNot.3: A problem has an immediate negative impact; this is a request, not harm.

C.q: A tester finds that a finished component will not meet its agreed quality specification. Which issue type is this, and which practice deals with it?
options: Request for change; the plans practice
C.why: A product that will not meet its quality specification is an off-specification, and issues are collected, assessed and controlled by the issues practice (11.1, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: Nobody has proposed a baseline change, and the plans practice does not control issues.
whyNot.1: The quality practice defines requirements and checks products, but the issue itself is handled in the issues practice, and its type is off-specification.
whyNot.3: Missing a specification is not a positive consequence, and the risk practice manages uncertainties, not issues.

C.q: How does PRINCE2 Agile tailor the issue management approach for agile working?
options: It treats change as a sign of poor planning to be kept low
It treats inevitable change as something to embrace and support
It requires every change to go to the board before work continues
It replaces the approach with the Agilometer for change requests
C.why: Iterative and incremental work produces many product versions and inevitable change, which the approach says should be embraced and supported (Table 11.1).

whyNot.0: Agile expects change; it is not treated as a planning failure.
whyNot.2: Changes within the baseline are handled at team level without going to the board.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer is a risk tool for agile working; it does not handle change requests.

C.q: An issue is raised that will not alter the project backlog. How and where is it handled?
C.why: Issues that do not affect the agreed baseline can be handled informally at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: The board decides issues that affect the baseline, not those within it.
whyNot.1: An exception report is for a forecast breach of tolerance, not every issue.
whyNot.2: The agile coach removes organization-level blockers; team-level issues stay with the team and PO.

reteach.title: Four kinds of post
reteach.question: If issues arrived as letters on the project manager's desk, how would you sort them?

blocks.body: A letter asking for something different is a request for change. A delivery note saying a product failed inspection is an off-specification. A bill you did not expect is a problem. A cheque you did not expect is a business opportunity. Every letter has already arrived, so each is an issue, not a risk. Then ask: does this one change the agreed project backlog?

blocks.text: Wants something changed = request for change. Will miss its spec = off-specification. Hurts now = problem. Unexpected upside = business opportunity.

explain.body: A proposal to change a baseline. Requests for change usually come from users and represent new or changed requirements.

test.q: Identify the missing words in the following sentence. A [?] is a proposal for a change to a baseline.
test.why: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: A business opportunity is an unexpected positive consequence.
whyNot.2: A problem is an issue with immediate negative impact.
whyNot.3: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification.

explain.body: A product that will not meet its quality specification: something built, or about to be built, that falls short of what was agreed.

test.q: A report built in iteration 3 will not meet the response time set in its quality specification. Which issue type is this?
test.why: A product that will not meet its quality specification is an off-specification (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: Nobody is proposing a change; the product is falling short of what was agreed.
whyNot.1: A shortfall is not a positive consequence.
whyNot.2: The specific type for a product missing its specification is off-specification.

explain.body: A problem has an immediate and negative impact, such as a supplier going bankrupt. A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence, such as extra funding.

test.q: Which issue type represents an unanticipated positive consequence for the project or user organization?
test.why: A business opportunity is an issue representing an unanticipated positive consequence (11.3.1).

whyNot.1: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline.
whyNot.2: An off-specification is a product missing its quality specification.
whyNot.3: A problem has an immediate negative impact.

explain.body: Agile produces many product versions, so change is inevitable. The issue management approach says it should be embraced and supported, and handled at team level unless it affects the baseline.

test.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile expect change during a project?
options: Because the board reviews scope at each daily stand-up
Because the project canvas is rewritten every iteration
Because iterative delivery produces many product versions
Because time and cost are flexed to absorb new work
test.why: The iterative and incremental nature of agile results in multiple product versions and inevitable change, which should be embraced (Table 11.1).

whyNot.0: The board does not attend stand-ups or review scope daily.
whyNot.1: The project canvas is refined at set points, not rewritten every iteration.
whyNot.3: Time and cost are fixed by default; scope flexes instead.
